title: THE FAMILY SECRET GOD REFUSED TO KEEP: WHY DID GOD FORBID SEX BETWEEN CLOSE RELATIVES WHEN EVEN BIBLICAL FAMILIES HAD PRACTICED IT?
paragraphs: THE FAMILY SECRET GOD REFUSED TO KEEP: WHY DID GOD FORBID SEX BETWEEN CLOSE RELATIVES WHEN EVEN BIBLICAL FAMILIES HAD PRACTICED IT?

Before God gave Israel the laws of Leviticus 18, some of the most important families in Scripture had already crossed boundaries that would later be forbidden. Was God changing His mind? Was He overlooking sin? Or was He revealing something about human intimacy, family betrayal, holiness, and grace that we desperately need to understand today?
“None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD.” — Leviticus 18:6 (ESV)
There is something deeply unsettling hidden in the family histories of the Bible.
Abraham married Sarah, his half-sister.
Jacob married two sisters, Leah and Rachel.
Lot's daughters became pregnant by their own father after getting him drunk.
And then, generations later, God spoke through Moses and declared that sexual relationships between close relatives were forbidden.
Wait.
Read that again.
The same Bible that records those ancient relationships also contains God's unmistakable command against them.
And if you have ever read Scripture carefully enough to notice that tension, you may have wondered something you were afraid to ask out loud.
Why would God forbid something that people in earlier biblical generations had practiced?
Did God's standards change?
Were those relationships acceptable before Moses?

And what about the uncomfortable question people often raise about Adam and Eve's children? If humanity began with one family, how could the earliest generations have multiplied without close relatives marrying?
These are not foolish questions.
They are questions that deserve more than a religious slogan, a frightening warning, or an answer that pretends every difficulty in Scripture disappears when we quote a verse.
Because when we study Leviticus 18 honestly, something extraordinary emerges.
We discover that God's commands concerning sexual boundaries are not simply about restricting desire.

They are also about protecting the vulnerable, preserving the integrity of family relationships, confronting the misuse of power, and teaching His people that love must never become an excuse for violating what is holy.
And underneath this difficult passage is a truth that reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
Not everything that happened in a biblical family was approved by the God who loved that family.
That distinction changes everything.
Imagine growing up in a household where the people who were supposed to protect you were the very people who made you afraid.
Imagine the confusion of discovering that someone could use the language of love while crossing a boundary that love itself should have protected.
Imagine carrying a family secret so heavy that even years later, hearing the word home does not bring comfort.
For some readers, this subject is an intellectual question.
For others, it touches a wound they have spent their entire lives trying to hide.
And that is why we must approach this passage carefully.
Not with sensationalism.
Not with condemnation toward those who have been harmed.
And certainly not with the dangerous assumption that everyone involved in a sexual relationship within a family had equal freedom, equal power, or equal responsibility.
God sees what people conceal.
He sees the difference between willing wrongdoing and exploitation.
He sees the child who could not consent, the vulnerable person who was manipulated, and the survivor who has spent years believing a lie about their own guilt.
The God who speaks in Leviticus is not indifferent to any of them.
But to understand why these commands appear where they do, we must first enter the world in which they were given.
Israel had been delivered from Egypt.
For generations, the Israelites had lived surrounded by a culture whose religious and social practices did not always reflect the holiness of the God who had rescued them.
Now they were being formed into a covenant people.
They were learning that freedom from slavery was not the same thing as freedom to live without moral boundaries.
God had brought them out of Egypt.
But Egypt's ways still had to be confronted.
In Leviticus 18:3, the Lord warned Israel not to imitate the practices of Egypt or Canaan. In verse 4, He commanded them to follow His judgments and statutes.
Then came the solemn declaration in verse 6.
In the Hebrew text, the central prohibition reads:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
Ish ish el-kol she'er besaro lo tiqrevu legalot ervah.
In context, this means:
“None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness.”
The expression she'er besaro refers to close kinship, literally conveying the idea of one's own flesh or near family relation.
The expression legalot ervah, “to uncover nakedness,” is a Hebrew idiom used in this chapter for prohibited sexual exposure or relations.
This is not merely a warning about accidentally seeing someone without clothing.
The chapter is establishing sexual boundaries within family relationships.
And the command ends with words that appear repeatedly throughout the holiness laws:
אֲנִי יְהוָה — Ani YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
That ending matters.
God was not presenting these boundaries as a matter of changing fashion, social embarrassment, or personal preference.
He was speaking as Israel's covenant Lord.
His people were not free to define holiness merely by what surrounding societies permitted.
And they were not free to call something righteous simply because their ancestors had done it.
Now comes the difficult part.
What do we do with Abraham?
Genesis 20:12 records Abraham explaining that Sarah was his father's daughter, though not his mother's daughter.
In other words, according to Abraham's own account, Sarah was his half-sister.
Yet Leviticus 18:9 explicitly prohibits sexual relations with a sister, whether she is the daughter of one's father or one's mother.
How do we reconcile that?
First, we must recognize that Abraham lived centuries before the Mosaic covenant and the giving of the Levitical law.
The Bible does not portray him as living under the specific legal code later delivered to Israel at Sinai.
But this does not automatically establish that every action of Abraham was morally ideal or that God approved of every aspect of his marriage.
The Bible's description of an event is not necessarily God's endorsement of it.
That is one of the most important principles for reading biblical narratives responsibly.
Scripture tells us that Abraham lied about his marital relationship out of fear.
It tells us that Jacob's household was torn by jealousy and rivalry.
It tells us that David committed adultery and arranged a man's death.
The fact that God continued working through these people does not transform their every decision into a divine example.
God's faithfulness to His promises is not proof that human beings have lived flawlessly.
Sometimes the most astonishing thing about the Bible is not how righteous its central human characters appear.
It is how honestly their failures are exposed.
Jacob's story is another striking example.
He married Leah and Rachel, two sisters.
Yet Leviticus 18:18 later prohibits taking a woman as a rival wife to her sister while the first sister is alive.
Read Genesis carefully, and the pain within that family becomes impossible to ignore.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel struggles with infertility.
Competition and resentment poison relationships that should have been marked by tenderness.
The narrative does not present their household as a peaceful model of family harmony.
It shows the suffering that unfolded within it.
Still, we must be precise: the existence of suffering in a biblical story does not, by itself, prove the precise reason for every later command.
What we can say is that the Bible does not require us to romanticize those arrangements.
It allows us to see their brokenness.
And that brings us to Lot.
Genesis 19:30–38 records one of the most disturbing episodes in the Old Testament.
Lot's daughters, fearing the loss of their family line, made their father drunk and had sexual relations with him without his informed participation.
The account is deeply troubling.
It is not a romance.
It is not an example to imitate.
And it is not presented as a command from God.
It is a narrative of desperation, deception, and a devastating violation of sexual boundaries.
When Leviticus later explicitly forbids such relations, we should not imagine that the earlier account was therefore being celebrated.
The Bible can preserve the truth about human darkness without asking us to admire it.
But perhaps you are still thinking about the question that reaches even further back.
Adam and Eve.
If they were the first human couple, and if their children formed the earliest human families, how did humanity multiply?
Genesis 5:4 tells us that Adam had other sons and daughters.
Under a reading of Genesis in which all humanity descends immediately from a single original couple, marriages among close relatives would appear necessary in the earliest generations.
That is a reasonable inference within that interpretation.
But we must be equally honest about what the text does not say.
Genesis does not provide a detailed marriage register for Adam's children.
It does not explicitly explain the precise relationships of Cain's wife or establish a complete system of early marriage rules.
And it does not directly state that God temporarily authorized incestuous marriages before later withdrawing that authorization.
Some Christians propose that close-relative marriage was initially permitted and later forbidden as human circumstances changed. Others approach the early Genesis genealogies differently.
These interpretations should not be confused with explicit statements of Scripture.
We must never pretend that our explanations are as authoritative as God's written Word.
The Bible gives us enough clarity to understand the command in Leviticus 18, even when it does not answer every historical question about the earliest generations.
And that distinction is not weakness.
It is reverence.
Faith does not require us to manufacture certainty where Scripture has not supplied it.
Now consider what Leviticus 18:6–18 actually does.
It does not merely prohibit one relationship.
It systematically identifies family boundaries.
Relations involving parents, siblings, grandchildren, aunts, certain in-laws, and other specified kinship connections are addressed.
Some prohibitions involve blood relationships.
Others concern relationships created by marriage.
The passage recognizes that family structures carry obligations that sexual desire must not override.
A parent is not merely another possible romantic partner.
A sibling relationship is not simply a friendship that can become sexual if both people desire it.
The family is a place where trust, dependency, authority, affection, and vulnerability intersect.
Sexualizing those relationships can profoundly damage the very bonds through which people are meant to receive security and care.
Modern knowledge also recognizes additional concerns, including the elevated risk of certain recessive genetic disorders among children conceived by close biological relatives.
That is a legitimate medical consideration.
But we should not claim that genetics is the stated reason for God's command in Leviticus.
The chapter does not give a genetic explanation.
Its explicit framework concerns holiness, prohibited sexual relations, and Israel's separation from the practices of surrounding nations.
We can recognize modern biological concerns without forcing scientific claims into a passage that does not make them.
The deeper theological principle remains powerful.
Human desire does not become holy simply because it feels powerful.
And affection does not automatically make a relationship righteous.
Sometimes what people call love is actually possession.
Sometimes what they call intimacy is exploitation.
Sometimes what they call a family secret is a wound that has been passed from one generation to the next.
But biblical love does not demand the surrender of another person's dignity.
Love protects.
Love refuses to exploit vulnerability.
Love does not use authority, dependence, fear, or silence to obtain what should never be taken.
This is why the broader witness of Scripture matters.
Psalm 82:3–4 calls for justice for the weak and the fatherless and for deliverance of the needy from the hand of the wicked.
Jesus Himself warned severely against causing the vulnerable to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
And when the apostle Paul addressed a sexual relationship involving a man and his father's wife in 1 Corinthians 5:1–5, he did not treat it as a harmless matter of private preference.
He called the church to take sexual wrongdoing seriously.
The New Testament does not present the coming of Christ as permission to disregard holiness.
Grace does not turn exploitation into love.
Forgiveness does not make wrongdoing harmless.
And redemption never requires victims to pretend that what happened to them was acceptable.
Perhaps that is where this article becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading these words have never committed the kind of sin described in Leviticus 18.
But they have been sinned against.
They were children.
They were vulnerable.
They trusted someone.
And someone betrayed that trust.
Maybe the person responsible was respected in the community.
Maybe that person quoted Scripture.
Maybe they prayed in public, served in church, or told everyone that family problems should never leave the home.
And perhaps you were told that speaking about what happened would destroy the family.
So you learned to smile.
You learned to function.
You learned to carry shame that never belonged to you.
If that is part of your story, please hear this clearly.
What someone did to you does not make you morally guilty of their actions.
You are not spiritually defiled because another person violated your boundaries.
You do not need to repent for being abused.
And the Gospel does not require you to return to an unsafe situation, conceal a crime, or offer someone renewed access to you in order to prove that you have forgiven them.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Reconciliation requires truth, accountability, and safety. In some circumstances, restored personal contact may never be wise or possible.
Where abuse has occurred, seeking appropriate protection, professional care, and lawful accountability is not a betrayal of Christian faith.
The God of truth does not need lies to protect His reputation.
And the church must never confuse protecting an institution with protecting the people entrusted to its care.
But there is another reader.
Someone who knowingly crossed a sexual boundary.
Someone who has hidden wrongdoing behind excuses, rationalizations, or years of silence.
For that person, the message is different, but the invitation of Christ is still real.
Do not call darkness light.
Do not use grace as permission to continue harming others.
Do not confuse feeling sorry with genuine repentance.
Biblical repentance involves turning away from sin, telling the truth, accepting appropriate consequences, and taking responsibility for the harm caused.
Where a crime has been committed, spiritual language must never be used to obstruct justice.
And where another person has been harmed, repentance does not entitle the offender to forgiveness on demand, restored trust, or renewed access to that person's life.
Yet even here, the Gospel confronts us with something extraordinary.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
Not by erasing justice.
Not by calling evil good.
But by bearing sin's judgment through His sacrificial death and opening the way to forgiveness and new life for those who repent and believe.
The cross is not evidence that God takes sin lightly.
It is evidence of how seriously He takes it—and how immeasurably great His mercy is.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (ESV)
Notice the timing.
Christ did not wait until humanity became worthy.
He came while we were sinners.
But His grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and live upright, godly lives.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant evil.
It is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches His people a new way to live.
This is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a memorable phrase.
But understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
He does not rewrite a victim's story by demanding silence.
He does not rewrite an offender's story by removing the need for repentance.
He rewrites lives through truth, mercy, justice, forgiveness, and transformation.
He brings what was hidden into the light.
He restores dignity to the wounded.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He gives hope where shame once appeared to have the final word.
And He offers a new identity that is not determined by the worst thing someone suffered or the worst thing a repentant sinner once did.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
The crowd wanted a public spectacle.
They wanted judgment.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of her accusers, refused to participate in their cruelty, and told the woman to leave her life of sin.

The passage, whose textual history is debated because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, has long been cherished by Christians for its portrayal of mercy joined to moral seriousness.
Its message resonates with truths clearly taught throughout the New Testament.
Jesus is neither indifferent to sin nor eager to destroy the repentant.
And in John 4, He speaks with a Samaritan woman whose complicated marital history becomes part of a conversation about living water and true worship.
He does not reduce her entire identity to her relationships.
He directs her attention to the gift of God.
This is the Savior we proclaim.
Holy enough to confront what destroys us.
Merciful enough to receive those who come to Him.
Powerful enough to begin a work of transformation no human being could accomplish alone.
And now return to the question that began this journey.
Why did God forbid sexual relationships with close relatives, even though earlier biblical families sometimes practiced them?
Because the giving of the law to Israel established explicit boundaries for God's covenant people, including boundaries that distinguished them from surrounding nations.
Because Scripture's record of earlier practices is not the same thing as a divine endorsement of those practices.
Because family relationships carry responsibilities that must not be surrendered to sexual desire.
And because God's call to holiness reaches into the places where human beings are most capable of both extraordinary tenderness and devastating betrayal.
We should not claim to know every unstated reason behind each prohibition.
But we can affirm what the text clearly teaches.
God did not leave Israel free to decide that every form of intimacy was acceptable.
He called His people to honor the boundaries He had established.
And through the fuller revelation of Jesus Christ, Christians are called not merely to avoid outward wrongdoing, but to love others with purity, truth, humility, and self-giving care.
The central question is no longer merely, “What did ancient families do?”
It is also, “Will I allow the Word of God to correct what my culture, my history, or my desires have taught me to accept?”
Because sometimes the hardest part of following Jesus is discovering that something familiar is not necessarily faithful.
Sometimes an inherited practice must be rejected.
Sometimes a family secret must be brought into the light.
Sometimes repentance begins with finally admitting, “What I called love was not love.”
And sometimes healing begins with the words, “What happened to me was wrong, and I do not have to carry the shame anymore.”
Maybe this article has answered a question you have carried for years.
Maybe it has challenged an assumption you never examined.
Or maybe it has touched a place in your life that still needs the healing presence of Christ.
Wherever you find yourself, do not run from the truth.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need to repent, come honestly.
If you need protection, seek it without shame.
If you need help, reach out to safe, trustworthy people who will take your concerns seriously.
If you are struggling to understand Scripture, keep studying.
And if you have been wounded, remember that healing does not have to happen on someone else's timetable.
Jesus is not frightened by difficult questions.
He is not embarrassed by the truth.
And His invitation to come to Him is not reserved for people with uncomplicated stories.
There is a reason Gospel Warrior continues to speak about the passages others sometimes avoid.
Because people are asking questions.
Because families are hurting.
Because believers need more than inspirational quotations.
Because the church needs disciples who can distinguish biblical truth from cultural assumptions, grace from permissiveness, and forgiveness from the concealment of harm.
And because somewhere, someone is one honest encounter with Scripture away from realizing that the Gospel is deeper than they ever imagined.
If this article opened your eyes, please do not allow the conversation to end here.

Some truths deserve more than a hurried reading. Return to Leviticus 18, Genesis 20, Genesis 29, 1 Corinthians 5, and the Gospel passages we have considered. Open your Bible. Examine the context. Let Scripture shape your convictions.
I also want to hear from you.
And if this strengthened your faith, share a Scripture that has helped you understand God's holiness or His mercy. Your testimony may encourage someone else to open the Bible again.
Our mission is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, conviction, repentance, encouragement, biblical understanding, and the life-changing truth of the Gospel.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth.
For believers who choose to give as part of their worship and stewardship, supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of generosity.
But we want to be biblically clear.
Your responsibility to your local church, your family, and those in need should not be neglected.
You can still help.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your sharing of sound biblical teaching matters.
Your willingness to help someone encounter Jesus matters.
But the greatest reward of supporting Gospel work is not merchandise.
It is knowing that your generosity is helping sustain a ministry dedicated to proclaiming Christ, encouraging discipleship, and making biblical resources available to others.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what money could never buy.
And no amount of engagement, public support, or religious activity can replace repentance and faith in Him.
That is why we will continue pointing back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Back to the Word of God.
Back to the Savior who does not excuse evil but can redeem lives devastated by it.
Perhaps you arrived at this article curious about ancient marriage practices.
Perhaps you expected an argument about genetics, history, or biblical law.
But I hope you leave with something more.
A deeper respect for the holiness of God.
A clearer understanding of the difference between biblical history and biblical commands.
A renewed commitment to protect the vulnerable.
And a stronger confidence that the Gospel of Jesus Christ is sufficient to confront the truth without surrendering hope.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its families.
It exposes them within the unfolding story of God's dealings with humanity.
And through that story, it ultimately directs our eyes toward the One who entered our broken world without becoming part of its sin.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was betrayed but never became a betrayer.
The One who was wounded but never used His power to exploit the weak.
The One who bore the cross and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, captives could find hope, and those who trust Him could receive new life.
He is not merely the answer to an uncomfortable Bible question.
He is the hope of a world filled with uncomfortable truths.
And when everything hidden is finally brought into the light, the greatest hope of the Gospel will remain:
Your family's darkest chapter does not have to become the final sentence of your story—because the final word belongs to Jesus Christ.
